Wish you had mentioned that overlevering an asset, even with positive expected return, can decrease geometric returns. There is an optimal leverage point, where increases in excess of this diminish geometric returns. This is described by the Kelly criterion and Merton share.

Positions sizing matters. Depending on your market assumptions on expected returns and volatilty, 3X or even 2X leverage may be beyond this point, introducing extra volatility for no gain to the investor. 

Including human capital as part of the balance sheet is impractical because investors cannot cash it in/borrow against it to rebalance in a margin call or crash.
SIZING is everything -  Leverage with BAD sizing will lead to portfolio implosion. (accounting for fund costs, premiums, opportunity costs)

My rationale for going all in on TQQQ:
Lump sum and DCA are very different games. With lump sump, you only care about the start and end points, what happens in between is irrelevant. With DCA, the path matters. You're buying at the harmonic price of the finite number of investments you put in. Because the harmonic mean is highly biased towards the lowest value, an investment path with more volatility will most likely have a lower harmonic mean and thus a higher rate of return (provided the endpoint is the same for all investment paths). Basically, *if you're going to DCA, it's more profitable to do it in an asset that has more volatility* In fact, with DCA, it's possible to make a profit even when the net market movement is zero or negative. Leveraged ETFs have high volatility and thus are ideal for DCA. Even if TQQQ had the same CAGR as SPY, it would still be a better choice for DCA because of its higher volatility.

Perhaps I can explain it somewhat intuitively. When you DCA, you always buy the same dollar value of the stock, regardless of the stock price. TQQQ is at ~$80 right now. Now if SPY had also been at $80, it would've only dropped to say, $60 max. Meaning instead of 10 shares, you can buy 13.33 shares. That's still nice but nowhere as nice as TQQQ. This happens because SPY isn't nearly as volatile as TQQQ and thus doesn't fluctuate a lot in either direction. Hence my claim (which I think is true) that DCA favors volatility.

It's fairly strange to make a video like this without mentioning once the Kelly formula. For any asset, if we know the expected future returns, volatility, cost of borrowing, cost of managing the asset / ter (and after making a small provision for market frictions), there is an EXACT formula to deterime the leverage factor which results in the highest expected returns. This would be known as "full Kelly" but typically, a more conservative "half-Kelly" is advised. I'm trying to put together the framework that Ben described in the video. 
You should use leverage if:
- You are young
- You have a small capital pool to invest
- You have high risk tolerance, higher than you need for just holding an index fund. (Potentially higher even than that needed to hold factor-tilted funds?)
- Your human capital is bond-like. Your employment and income are stable, and have weak correlation to the stock market or general economic performance. You should think carefully if your work and life situations really are as stable as you think. The more the returns to your human capital are subject to changes in the stock market or general economic conditions, the less leverage you can afford to take on.
- You accept that leverage amplifies volatility, and amplifies both the upside and downside of the returns (e.g. your investment can fall 70-80% during market crashes); and are prepared not to sell during a downturn. [I would add that you want to have an emergency fund to avoid having to sell your investment during a personal or financial crisis].
- You accept that, depending on the direction of the market, leverage can actually underperform the underlying asset, particularly during a falling or choppy market.

Regarding the leveraged product, it should:
- be buying a diversified stock portfolio, not a single stock
- have low operating expenses 
- have low borrowing cost (less than or equal to 1.5% above the risk-free rate). You need to find out this detail because the borrowing cost is not typically included in the operating expense ratio.
- You don't need to be afraid of the daily rebalancing. It doesn't automatically lead to erosion of return.
- You should be aware that with higher leverage, and thus higher volatility, the return you need to break even increases more than you expect. For every 1% increase in daily volatility, the break-even percentage is roughly doubled.

Also, I've been using descriptive terms like 'low operating expenses', 'young ', and 'small capital pool'. It would be great if Ben or people in the comments could attach some numbers to these terms.
